name: Waray Sorsogon
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Zorc, R. David. 1977. The Bisayan Dialects of the Philippines: Subgrouping and Reconstruction. Pacific Linguistics C-44 (covers Sorsogon Bisakol; accent treated throughout)
earlier_scan.note: Glottolog MED has only McFarland 1974 wordlist; Zorc 1977 plausibly covers Waray Sorsogon accent but sealang/PL scans unreachable (cert expired)

new_statements.quote: The stress is usually found in the last or penultimate syllable as in ma.a.ri.NGA.sa, ma.PU.yo, ma.his.DAL, ma.pi.NI.ton, ma.ra.MO.kon, a.WA.ton, ha.ra.rag.YO, mag.ka.ra.MANG.hod, da.ra.non.DA.non, ka.HI.ran, ka.U.pod, GING.ot, ma.YAD, mag.LI.wan, mag.re.LAN.si, in.hi.HI.mo, nag.U.u.yag, ba.RA.tog, in.nga.nga.RAT, KA.wat. [...] However, when a suffix is appended, the stress is typically put at the penultimate syllable as in ma.pi.NI.ton, ma.ra.MO.kon. [...] When the accent is placed with open syllables, it combines stress and length, whereas it merely combines stress elsewhere. [...] The second to last syllable is identified as the location of the stress.
new_statements.citation: San Jose, Dominic Bryan S. & John Gerald A. Pilar. 2023. Phonological idiosyncrasies of the Southern Sorsogon dialect in Bulan, Philippines. Rupkatha Journal on Interdisciplinary Studies in Humanities 15(3), article 05. DOI 10.21659/rupkatha.v15n3.05
new_statements.locator: §4.1, pp. 6-7 (first two sentences); §4.2, p. 8 (third sentence); §5 Conclusion, p. 15 (last sentence)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically placed on either the penultimate or the final syllable (contrastive: ma.PU.yo 'quiet' vs MA.pu.yo 'to be quiet'; Zorc's Bisayan-wide pair pu:nuq 'tree trunk' vs punuq 'full'); the penult is the default/most frequent site, and suffixation (e.g. -on) draws stress onto the new penult. A stressed open penult is also long; stress on a closed syllable carries no length. Zorc 1977 adds for all Bisayan dialects incl. Gubat that a closed penult is always stressed, so stress is predictable only for that shape.
new_statements.exceptions: San Jose & Pilar: several adjectives are final-stressed (sa.rag.DAY, ma.his.DAL, hu.BOG, ma.YAD); some verb derivations move stress to the first syllable of the word (MA.a.ri.nga.sa, MA.his.dal) - plausibly a long verbal prefix; a few forms in their Table 1 (ma.a.ri.NGA.sa, ma.ra.MO.kon) contradict the 'last or penultimate' summary only in that they are penult of a longer word. Zorc 1977: stress pattern is overridden by exclamatory intonation (pp. 50-51); antepenult length occurs in Masbate/Sorsogon/Waray-area dialects (p. 216, p. 245).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms from interviews and a word list (Bulan municipality speakers); San Jose & Pilar mark stress in capitals on syllabified words, not phrases. Zorc treats accent as a word-level lexical property but notes phrase-level intonational overrides.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement of record describes the Bulan-municipality variety of Southern Sorsogon; San Jose & Pilar call it a "dialect" of Bikol, but Bulan is one of the srv municipalities (Gubat, Barcelona, Bulusan, Santa Magdalena, Matnog, Bulan, Irosin) and Lobel 2013 uses Bulan as his Southern Sorsoganon reference dialect, so it is wara1299 [srv]. Zorc 1977's dialect 'Gub' (Gubat, Southern Sorsogon) is the same language; his 'Sor' (Northern Sorsogon, sursugunun) is Masbate Sorsogon [bks], a different Glottolog language. ISO CR 2009-063 (2010) renamed srv from 'Sorsogon, Waray' to 'Sorsoganon, Southern'.

sources.locator: §4.1, pp. 6-7 (first two sentences); §4.2, p. 8 (third sentence); §5 Conclusion, p. 15 (last sentence)
sources.note: First-hand (6 Bulan speakers): stress falls on the last or the penultimate syllable, lexically; conclusion names the penult as the location of stress; accent on an open syllable = stress + length, elsewhere stress only; changing accent placement (e.g. ma.PU.yo 'quiet' vs MA.pu.yo 'to be quiet') changes meaning; final-stressed words sound 'loud/angry' to outsiders (pp. 6-8, 15).

sources.citation: Zorc, R. David Paul. 1977. The Bisayan Dialects of the Philippines: Subgrouping and Reconstruction. Pacific Linguistics C-44. Canberra: ANU. (dialect 'Gub' = Gubat dialect of Southern Sorsogon, data from McFarland 1974)
sources.note: Survey statement for all 36 Bisayan dialects incl. Gub: accent is phonemic (penult vs ultima, e.g. pu:nuq 'tree trunk' vs punuq 'full', pp. 216-217); accented open penult is long, unaccented/closed syllables short, ultima short (p. 50); in all dialects studied (except Kuyonon) a closed penult is stressed, so stress is predictable from shape there (pp. 50, 218, 243); stress is 'a syntactic feature' overridable by intonation (pp. 50-51); Mas, Sor, N-S, S-L, War allow antepenult length (p. 216; Gub not listed).

sources.citation: de la Torre, Ryan G. & Gina O. Gonong. 2020. A phono-lexicostatistical analysis of Bikol-Sorsogon varieties. The Normal Lights 14(2): 28-61.
sources.note: Lexicostatistics of 11 Bikol-Sorsogon town varieties (incl. Gubat, Barcelona, Bulusan, Bulan); IPA forms carry stress marks ([ʔɪ.ˈrʊŋ] 'nose' Gub/Bar/Bulu/Bula, [ba.ˈlʊ.kaɡ] 'feather', [ˈtʊl.ʔaŋ] 'bone') and a 'stress shift' row, but suprasegmentals are explicitly ignored in the comparison; no rule stated.

sources.citation: Lobel, Jason William. 2013. Philippine and North Bornean languages: issues in description, subgrouping, and reconstruction. PhD diss., University of Hawai'i at Manoa.
sources.note: No stress statement for Southern Sorsoganon; it appears only in subgrouping tables and in angry-register data (Bulan dialect) written with accent marks (kakán, gútom, babáye, p. 198). Contrastive-accent section (8.2.9) concerns Manide/Inagta Alabat; footnote (p. 287) says some Bikol languages have lost contrastive stress (Lobel 2003).

sources.note: The only full descriptive survey of the Bikol-area Bisayan dialects (Sorsogon, Gubat, Masbate); Zorc 1977 draws all his Gubat data from it, so its phonology section is the primary basis for any accent statement on Waray Sorsogon and would supersede the 2023 article.
